rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch facts under control and turns the weakest claim into the story: "Anker says its home battery skips the rewiring — installers will decide if that's true." B has usable bones, but it opens by inflating one launch into a trend with "Consumer electronics makers are moving from your pocket to your electrical panel. Anker just set the timeline." That is the difference between a pitch a reporter can test and a conference-panel sentence looking for evidence.
gaps_in_A: "purchase measured in thousands of dollars and decades on the wall" overreaches the supplied facts; pricing is only partially disclosed and warranty terms are explicitly missing.

"the widely held position on this beat is that whole-home storage means electricians, panel work, and permitting" may be true beat context, but it is not in the update. Keep it as a proof target, not a stated fact.

"coming for the Tesla Powerwall" is a strong frame, but it depends on pricing, capacity, warranty, installer coverage, and orderability. A names those proof gaps, but the headline should stay provisional until they are filled.
gaps_in_B: "Consumer electronics makers are moving from your pocket to your electrical panel" invents a plural trend from a single Anker launch. One company is not a wave.

"Anker is betting homeowners skip home batteries because of the installation job, not the price" adds a false contrast. The update gives no adoption research and says pricing is only partially disclosed.
"the installation barrier has been cited repeatedly as the main friction point" is outside evidence presented as fact. Source it or cut it.
"value-oriented buyers" imports brand positioning that the update does not supply. Known for chargers is a fact; value-buyer psychology is not.
